sentences.en: What did Jensen represent to the broader AI market?
So when you take him out of the equation, who steps in to fill that gap of aggressive investment in AI?
So Jevons paradox where it's like you get this stuff cheaper, you find more uses for it, and then you expand across your uses.
Hello everyone and welcome back to another episode of the Brainstorm.
Today it is just Brett and I.
Sam is traveling, so we have lost our moderator, the voice of reason.
But we will begin we will begin with a discussion on SpaceX, some historic news over the weekend, and then we will get into Jensen and everything AI.
So Brett, why don't you kick us off?
Sure.
So SpaceX it the Starship number 42 and it's flight I think it was flight 16 of its Starship booster and rocket landed the top stage of its orbital rocket, which is historic.
This is the largest by volume object that we have ever returned from space.
So it's, you know, on a payload basis something like three 3x what the space shuttle was able to do.
It's also financially and strategically important for SpaceX.

We think that with reusable top stage, which we weren't sure was actually going to be possible, they could lower their costs per launch to around $100 per kilogram from right now we think on the Falcon 9 they're at,
You know, $600 to $700 per kilogram.
And on the Starship, if they couldn't reuse the top stage, they might have been able to get down to 500.
But this is a material lowering in their cost inputs.

It's also can allow them to accelerate their rate of progress because he Elon on inspecting the heat shield tiles on the on the on the top stage said we think we could turn this, refurbish it, and get it
Ready to again within a few weeks.
That's much better than we expected.
We thought the first Starship to even successfully land if it were to occur would have taken 90 days of refurbishment.
So their ship came in much better shape than we anticipated.

They landed We actually didn't think they would Even in the cases where they successfully land this thing, we thought it would take them six commercial launches before they could successfully land the top stage.
And you know, rather than taking three months to turn it, they think they can do it in a few weeks.

So it suggests kind of cost blended costs for launch for SpaceX, which is an important input into how much capital they have to put up front to launch their satellites to generate revenue on is coming in better than
Anticipated.
Not to mention the fact it was a totally mind-blowing and cool exhibition of engineering excellence.
So that's the net.
Brett, what is the main hurdle to refurbishment?
As in, you know, you you're lowering the amount of time it takes to turn the Starship around.
What exactly goes into that?

Well, like if you look at the Space Shuttle, they would literally have to inspect every single tile and then hand craft replacement tiles for any tiles that needed replacement and, you know, basically like do a custom kind of
Rebuild of the bottom of the of the Space Shuttle every time.
So Starship is it's roughly the same as in you look at all of the kind of like return surface, all of the protection layer and assess what needs to be taken off and built back in and was there
Any kind of infiltration damage to the stainless steel surface under the tiles?
And so, you know, conceptually you could you might have to replace all of the tiles if you don't have very good tiles and so then you would like basically take off the shell and put it back into kind
Of the manufacturing assembly line and put them all on.

What SpaceX has done here is one, they've made tiles much more robust relative to the space shuttle tiles and design them for manufacture and come up with a mechanism by which to put them on relatively inexpensively.
But if they only have to replace, you know, I don't know, 40 or 50 tiles, you know, then they could go through that pretty quickly.
And their aim is to get to something where it's like just really automated or you do an inspection and you know it's good to go.
One advantage they have over the space shuttle is for now there's no humans coming down in these things.
So you can actually take better you can take more risk because you're not putting any lives at risk.
It's just your own capital at risk if you have to divert offshore and crash it.
So I would expect that over time they'll like test the limits of how many you know how much damage the tiles can have and the ship still returns.

There's some optimization of like you know if you're reusing the ship five or six times and you have enough of them in inventory, then you actually are crossing some threshold where you're like, okay, this one we know it's
Not going to come back, but we're going to launch it anyway, you know, and then have it incinerate on reentry.
So when they're inspecting the heat shield, how do they assess whether or not, you know, specific tiles can be reused again?
And are the tiles meant to be reused for like how many do they expect how many reuses out of this specific heat shield do they expect to get per tile or for the tile specifically?
I don't know the answer to that latter question.

I you know I think in the overall answer is and this is call it general to Elon Musk Enterprises is they have I'm sure like a simulated expectation, but simulation runs into the you know fist of reality pretty
Quickly.

And so the value they got out of that previous starship landing and not exploding was actually being able to physically inspect and say, okay, how much if we were to replace these, how many would we need to replace?
Where would we need to replace them?
And how can we kind of design so there's less infiltration in those areas?

Same with this ship that comes back as in they're going to, you know, look at the entire surface, assess where kind of they can make improvements, use the actual lived data to make additional improvements to the ship and
It should increase their, you know, turn rate and ability to economically do this thing.
And I think that's a certainly relative to the, you know, over the weekend there was also the United Launch Alliance's Amazon carrying rocket failed to get into orbit.
Its upper stage engine seemed to fail in an unexpected way or maybe, you know, its engines failed in an unexpected way.
And there's just like the they have so much less data.
I mean they got data from this flight, but you know, they just don't have the launch cadence to gather the data to improve to do more launches to gather the data to improve.

And so you know, the fact that SpaceX is now going to get into a place where they're with less capital they're going to get accelerated amounts of data from doing continued launches means that they should also increase their
You know, capital efficiency and ability to know like where the limits are for the craft.
Mhm.
And this will be a question that will probably segue us into our next topic, which is Jensen out.
But how do you think about this relative to the opportunity surrounding orbital compute?
What is this unlock when it comes to, you know, being able to set up data centers in space?
Yeah, I so we've previously talked about crossing the around $300 $400 per kilogram threshold is where the unit economics of a data center in space begin to pencil.
You know, that's subject to a lot of other unknowns, like cost to manufacture the satellite and cost of chips put in it, but that was a keep cost input.
And as you get down into the $100 a kilogram and below, that as an important cost input just falls out of the equation.
And I think it's very likely that the limiter on compute in space is no longer kind of launch or launch vehicle availability.
That's the other like piece of this.

If you're reusing the rockets, you know, they have a whole factory set up to manufacture these Starship rockets, which nobody has ever really done in rocketry, at least for manufacturing scale the way they have.
And now they're going to begin to reuse them.
And so their inventory of available potential launch vehicles in terms of like launch mass to orbit is just going to explode.

And so in terms of if the competition in compute is one, if there is not unlimited, but this huge demand for compute, which we think there is, the market is less certain of that, then kind of like SpaceX
Definitely has cornered the market on being able to do compute at scale.

As in it's highly likely that they'll be able to do a lot more and continue to grow it relative to themselves and others trying to operate on the ground, identify sites, negotiate with municipalities, get kind of like the
All of the complex negotiations in place to build these individual data centers.
And so this is seems clearly the way to manufacture compute at scale quickly.
Mhm.
But let's turn to Nvidia.
Nick, I'd be curious to hear your opinion.
Jensen is now officially out.
Lots of ramifications for like the entire industry, world, etc.
What do you think about kind of like what it means for Nvidia, what it means for buyers of compute, what it means for the ecosystem and venture?
What do you think?
Yeah, I think my big takeaway here is, you know, what did Jensen represent to the broader AI market?

Like, we can put, you know, just the discussion around Nvidia on pause because I think the ramifications for the broader AI ecosystem are more interesting to speak to because I think what he represented was this aggressive investment approach
To scaling AI.

And so I think what people are rightly concerned with right now is what is the reflexive response by the industry when you take this central figure out of the equation that was investing in, you know, AI genomics plays,

Which was potentially providing backstops for the neo cloud business, which he essentially propped up the neo cloud business because his allocation to those companies over the traditional cloud providers supported the, you know, early growth of those companies.
So when you take him out of the equation, well, who steps in to fill that gap of aggressive investment in AI?

I think you're going to see and, you know, I sent you the note this morning, SemiAnalysis, which has been riding the call it the coattails of the AI trade and helping people distinguish right from wrong and, you know,
Where this market can head, just lowered their forecasts by I think roughly 28% for capex spend and, you know, you can delineate how that translates and what it means for ARR for the entire industry.
But I think, you know, people are trying to make sense of this.
There's a lot, you know, of conversation around the CFO.

Seems like her investment approach, which, you know, probably is what you want from a CFO, is completely different than Jensen, and she's going to take potentially a much more conservative stance on AI.
But, you know, we'll find out a lot tomorrow when they report.
And maybe we should bring Frank on next week to discuss if there's anything pretty interesting that comes out of that earnings, which I'm sure there will be.

But, you know, me, when I look at this, I say, you know, there's going to be some uncertainty in the market and that is going to cause, you know, delays and not just, you know, spend for data centers,
But how people approach AI generally.
I think he was that big and meant that much to the market.

Yeah, I think I think I would distinguish between things that are strategically rational for NVIDIA to do and the velocity at which they're trying to pursue those strategies and like as in I would expect that a you know,
A CFO leading the business might still conduct those strategically rational acts, but would do so at a more measured pace than he was trying to push essentially the balance sheet.
And so because the one way to interpret his set of actions is basically he was doing everything he could to create competition in other layers of the value chain.
As in the infrastructure as a service layer, like he talks about a five layer cake.
I think it's a useful way to think about kind of like the AI kind of stack.

There's other ways to think about it, but you have power, you basically have the chips, you have the infrastructure as a service guys, then you have the kind of like AI platforms, and then you have the applications built
On top of them.
And so if you think about where he was deploying resources, you know, he's occupying the chip layer, so he wants to maximize revenue or economic power to the chip layer.
So that means he needs additional infrastructure partners, not just AWS and Azure, right?
And so he injects capital into seeding these neo clouds that are going to be really good at accelerators to create more kind of buyers for his chips at that portion of the market.
Then at the model layer, you know, he needs it to not just be in the Anthropic and OpenAI game.

So he was kind of like helping SpaceX to bootstrap and he was investing heavily in enabling open source or open weight models because that provides a competitive kind of layer against those core frontier labs at that part of
The chip stack, including you know, allowing you know, infrastructure as service access to the chips in China is an important part of that creating these open weight models.

And so kind of the and then even at the application later directly investing in kind of venture startups in the biology space where there's this likely very large addressable market, but it's more kind of speculative as to how
We get there, but that could be a demand pull for chips because there's so much data in biology.
And so that's kind of how I think of how they were allocating.
I would think a CFO would say, well, that's all strategically rational.
It's just a question of how much am I levering up the balance sheet on the basis of the next 12 months of demand are going to be high enough across all of those different things, you know.

And I think particularly given the US regulatory I mean, he was basically forced out by the State Department, I think is broadly the reporting and probably right because they're concerned about Chinese companies getting access to these next gen
Chips even through kind of a cloud interface.

You know, that probably dampens or maybe just clamps down on that channel for NVIDIA chips, which was basically selling in chips to willing buyers who would then turn around and create tools out of those chips that provide you
Know, open weights that provides inference demand for those chips because you're not having to pay OpenAI and Anthropic service margin.
So like net of it all, I think you can expect certainly less venture funding from NVIDIA, assuming Jensen doesn't come back into this kind of multiomics type stuff.
You can expect like more measured financing of the near clouds potentially, though I think that's still strategically rational.
You can definitely expect that there's going to be difficulty for the at least Chinese companies getting access to next gen chips to keep open weight up with the frontier.

Maybe offset by you know, some US companies I mean, you know, OpenAI has an open weight model, but Meta, you know, potentially seeing an opportunity to actually go back into open weight, though Meta has pulled back to that
From that some degree.
So I think that's kind of like how I think of the kind of staggering implications.

And then there's I think there's this like so SpaceX, for instance, as a US buyer of chips, maybe they have more leverage over Nvidia because Nvidia doesn't have this Chinese channel to sell into anymore.
And certainly he had all these supply chain relationships below him that he had secured with handshakes where, you know, Google is out there being like, hey, you could package our chips.
We're a more reliable partner now cuz who knows what's happening with Nvidia because maybe they're not going to as aggressively spend.
And so it does shake up kind of like AMD probably doing the same set of actions.
It shakes up kind of the degree to which Nvidia had aligned all of the supply chain to allow them to continue to accelerate.
And so it probably does make it more likely over the medium term that Nvidia's, you know, share of kind of like the cutting edge diminishes.
I mean, I think that's like the full set of things here.

I think what will be interesting too, and you you've talked about this more from the lens of SpaceX where, you know, because SpaceX is able to bring compute on faster than most of its other competitors, they're the likely
Company that ends up finding, you know, where demand ultimately sits.

And I think because you're now and this might be more of a US specific story, but because you're now going to take all of those chips that were supposed to be allocated to China or were finding their way
Into China and it's all going to, you know, presumably stay in, you know, domestic territory in the US.
I think a lot of these companies are going to get their hands on the allocation they had seemingly been wanting.
And so I do think it will be interesting to see you might get a faster answer into what like true demand is there for, you know, GPUs.
I you know, I think one thing to watch is GPU rental pricing.

Like a lot of, I think outside of maybe power bottlenecks, you should have a lot more come online at least in the US because those chips, if there are willing buyers, they will, you know, be sold to them
Here, not make their way across the sea.
So I'm curious to see how that plays out.
And again, you know, when you are in a moment of scarcity, your indication for what you want, you I think we were listening to that Howard Marks call this morning with everyone on the team.
Always over order because it like the spot price is high and you don't want Yeah, of course.

So now we're going to find out the flip side of that and like where true demand actually is because I don't think you have that main figurehead being, you know, the leading force to like I think what Jensen
Was doing was that for NVIDIA for, you know, you know, going to TSMC and saying here's what we need and, you know, making it a huge number so that they remain 80% of the market.

Now if you have a CFO step in and say, well, we actually only need this amount because this is, you know, what we're what we're seeing, I think that changes, you know, everything in a very short amount of
Time.
And you'll find out.

Then it distills down to like those OpenAI, Anthropic, and you know, SpaceX's kind of call it AI software revenue collectively, you know, do they continue to accelerate at anything close to the historical pace of acceleration or was basically
The first half of the year differ, I think.
It's interesting.
Not interested.
I mean, we're usually on the opposite side of things, but I do I I'm more cautious around you know, ARR and demand at least in the next year than you are.

But curious, you know, you should Well, like I think there's two ways to one kind of your caution comes from the fact that, you know, Ford companies are saying to you like, hey, look, yes, this AI stuff is
Super useful and now we're figuring out how to efficiently extract, call it the capability out of it without as intense a set of AI spend.
And so what does that mean?

It means instead of like giving all their engineers access only to the frontier and the engineers just use the frontier and crank out tokens, we're aggressively developing our own harnesses so it shifts to the most efficient model for
The task.

And if you look at the ramp data on a on a like a blended weighted average adjusted for intelligence token basis, like the cost for intelligence to these companies has collapsed 97% year over year basically.
Something You know, it's basically like if you do all that, they've had this huge collapse in intelligence.

My confidence in part arises from that If you look at that same data, you know, there is a clear correlation between when they get cheaper per intelligence per like intelligence weighted tokens, these firms tend to spend more in
Aggregate, not less, blended across.
As in their token demand for every 1% drop in basically intelligence costs, you end up with a 1.2% increase in the total spend.
So Jevons Paradox where it's like you get this stuff cheaper, you find more uses for it, and then you expand across your uses.
And so that's the high-level like way I would think about the industry.
And I understand that people don't believe that.
As in they just don't.
And they don't There's a like And it some of it feels, but also there's an important like backward-looking reason they don't.
They look at Anthropic's revenue in particular and they say, well, you onboarded a bunch of revenue in the second quarter on a dollars basis and then in the third quarter you onboarded less.
So if we just assume like with a typical software business, I have a sales force, I say, go sell this product.
They go out, they're going to identify the best prospects first.
They're going to go to them, and those best prospects will like land them, and they'll land this much revenue.
And then they say, okay, now I'm going to the next best set of prospects.
They go out to that.
It's like smaller, slightly smaller, slightly harder to sell.
And so same sales force lands like this much revenue.
You naturally say, well, what's coming next?
It's an even harder set of prospects.
So then you would have it, you know, increment down again.
If you use that to like say, well, this is what the industry is going to do, you might end up with, you know, collectively like less than a trillion dollars in spend by 2030.
Like that's what you it would just like increment down that way.
Whereas, you know, if instead you say, look, on a dollars per compute basis, this is what they're monetizing at, and this is how much compute they have lined up.
And if you look over time, they've been monetizing better on a dollar per compute basis over time because they are delivering more intelligence per unit of compute.
And then you look at the planned compute they have on coming online, then you end up with this, you know, high single digit trillions in revenue by 2030.
And so it's really a question of is it a sales force selling AI or is it the intelligence itself of AI that's selling AI?
And I think it's a different beast.
Like as in I understand why a software as a service analyst would be like this is the way that software businesses work.
You have to have somebody go in and convince people to use it and then they use it and that's kind of it.
Because this is in a utilization base, so it's really usefulness based, I think that like the dynamics of how this sells in will play out very differently.
And I think we'll see like strong evidence and like what does Thropic's fourth quarter look like?
What does their commentary look like as they're coming to market?
But Yeah.
I think it's some in between of the two where, you know, the sales force is important to growth, but I do believe in what you're saying.
My bigger question is just, you know, yes, there are maybe infinite numbers of use cases to which you can deploy AI against.
But my question is when you distill down, you know, all of those use cases, what are the ones where companies are actually willing to pay top dollar?
And I think what we've seen over this last year is like the diffusion of AI into those categories was extremely fast because it is a very intuitive product for people that understand it.
That's why coding adoption, you know, AI coding solutions, you know, that technology was adopted extremely fast.
But I think what happens now is you get into, you know, a mode and a use of the technology where you're going to figure out whether or not it's actually worth to spend money on it.
As in you may still be using AI across your marketing and legal and X, Y and Z, but how much are you actually willing to pay for it is the big question.
And I just I think you have to have a few quarters, you have to you have to understand like put it this way, you can't have your AI spend continually outgrow your revenue growth.
So there is a gating factor into which you're offsetting it if you're offsetting it with cuts and spend somewhere else, but yes.
Yes, that is that is But I do think that takes potentially longer than the market expects because everyone's looking at this year and saying, well, this growth was staggering.
And if we play this out and, you know, there's a new model that comes out with a potential new use case and we see this next inflection point, then yes, you can get into this low single trillions of
Dollars in revenue.
I just think there's going to be bumps and hurdles along the way that the market may or may not be pricing in at the moment.
I think it's going to be, you know, you'll find out if what I'm saying or what you're saying is right or wrong within like the next two quarters.
Like I think it plays out, you know, given what's happening with Nvidia, like people are asking questions.
Is financially it'll look like I'm right, but the market will still disbelieve it.
That's where I think I think that's what's going to happen.
Yeah.
We will see.
We will see.
Yes.
All right.
All right.
Thank you everyone.
We will be back next week.

vocab.usage: the next two quarters 未來兩個季度；this quarter 本季
vocab.example: We will find out within the next two quarters.
vocab.example_zh: 未來兩個季度內就會知道答案。

vocab.usage: play out differently 發展得不同；think differently 用不同方式思考
vocab.example: The dynamics will play out very differently.
vocab.example_zh: 後續發展會非常不一樣。

vocab.usage: assuming (that)… 假設…；assuming he doesn't… 假設他不…
vocab.example: Assuming he does not come back, funding may slow.
vocab.example_zh: 假設他不回來，資金可能會放緩。

vocab.usage: interests in securities 證券中的利益；securities or issuers 證券或發行人
vocab.example: They may have financial interests in securities discussed here.
vocab.example_zh: 他們可能持有這裡討論到的證券。

vocab.usage: the accuracy or completeness 正確性或完整性；guarantee the accuracy 保證正確性
vocab.example: Ark does not guarantee the accuracy of third-party information.
vocab.example_zh: ARK 不保證第三方資訊的正確性。
